title: Maternal mortality and health policies in Sub-Saharan Africa insights from Nigeria Rwanda South Africa Gabon
Health Financing in the Republic of Gabon
Gabon indigents scheme: a social health insurance program for the poor.
abstract: Background: Despite global commitments under SDG-3, maternal mortality rates remain disproportionately high in Sub-Saharan Africa. This review examines how health policies have shaped outcomes between 2014 and 2024 in Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa, and Gabon. Methods: A comparative narrative review was conducted using WHO, World Bank, UNFPA, DHS, and national policy documents. Guided by the Walt & Gilson Policy Triangle and the WHO Health System Building Blocks, policies were assessed for context, content, actors, process, and health system capacity. Data were synthesized thematically to compare implementation and outcomes. Findings: Rwanda achieved substantial declines through decentralized financing, performance-based funding, and community health worker integration. South Africa reduced deaths via integration of HIV and maternal services but still faces equity gaps. Gabon improved financial access but rural infrastructure and workforce limitations constrain outcomes. Nigeria’s fragmented governance and weak PHC financing explain stagnation despite multiple reforms. Conclusion: Implementation quality, not policy presence, drives progress. Strengthening governance, financing transparency, workforce readiness, and community engagement remains crucial for achieving SDG-3. This study highlights cross-country lessons transferable to similar contexts. © The Author(s) 2026.

Assesses health financing in the Republic of Gabon in light of the government's introduction of a national health insurance program and its commitment to achieving universal health insurance coverage in the medium term. Discusses the background and objectives; health outcomes and the use of health services; health financing; the national health insurance program; assessing costs and options for bridging the coverage gaps; and key reform issues and policy options. Saleh is Senior Health Economist at the World Bank. Couttolenc is Chief Executive Officer of the Performa Institute. Barroy is Health Economist at the World Bank. Bibliography; no index.

This paper briefly describes primary health care and accessibility to health care provision in Gabon, and the social health insurance architecture of the GIS. The paper is not intended to provide an analytical and detailed study on health insurance in Gabon. It simply aims to provide a description the GIS in terms of eligibility criteria, targeting, and registration of beneficiaries; special topics related to the management of public funds of the social insurance of the GIS; management of the services offered; and financial sustainability of the GIS. It contributes to the Universal Health Coverage Studies Series on sharing experiences in the field of universal health coverage.
